subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition from constituents of mine resident in the area of Red Rock, Nipigon, and Dorion, who have signed a petition protesting that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
They believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised, in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations, that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised but that the trade deal negotiated by the Government actually threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to control foreign ownership effectively, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interest of Canadians, and to equalize opportunities among the regions.
Whereas the proposed trade agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future, the petitioners pray that the House of Commons might be dissolved so that the people of Canada would have an opportunity to accept or to reject this agreement with the American Government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-109, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to continue the debate on Bill C-109, an Act to provide the Government with a $25,300 million borrowing authority.
When I was addressing the Bill the last time the matter was before the House, I pointed out that the Government had failed to give arts and culture the kind of boost they need in terms of tax policy and, I would add at this point, in terms of the free trade negotiations.
Canadian arts and cultural industries deserve protection, not only for what they do in respect of our sovereign concerns but as well as for their importance to the Canadian economy and to employment. Statistics Canada has said that in 1987 the arts and cultural industries contributed $11 billion to the gross national product and that over one million Canadians drew income directly or indirectly from these industries, following a remarkable 90 per cent increase in the number of jobs in those sectors since 1971. It is mainly because of the social and cultural roles they play that these industries should have been better protected in the free trade talks.
To continue from the point where I was discussing what could have been the Government's economic thrust, I talked about the need for block averaging for artists, not just for farmers. In another area I was talking about arts organizations. They are designed to promote the arts and welfare of artists and should be accorded special status under the Income Tax Act, which would allow them to issue receipts giving tax deductions for gifts in the same way as registered Canadian amateur athletic associations do now. It is interesting that the Province of Quebec adopted a system akin to that recommended by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in January, 1987, but this system only applies with regard to Quebec organizations and Quebec taxation. Unfortunately no reference to this has been made by the Government in its White Paper. This issue still remains a high priority for the arts community.
In respect of money for national museums, two national museums are expected to open their facilities in Ottawa during 1988-89-the National Gallery and the Museum of Civilization. I had hoped that each of these museums would be adequately funded to meet the demands of the newer and bigger facilities and that consequently their acquisition budgets, particularly in the case of the National Gallery, would not be severely restricted. I had hoped that the Government would provide money for these important needs. Little did i expect that it would undertake to play a shell game and
Borrowing Authority
just move moneys within that pot. There have been no increases, just unfair manoeuvres which will negatively impact on other museums across the land. At the same time, the lack of concern and the lack of attention to the decision of the Cultural Properties Review Board respecting a piece of work by Gustav Klimt that the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts wished to purchase obviously indicates that the federal Government or the Minister missed the boat as they did not act on time.
In respect of Canadian programming on radio and television, it is essential to the enjoyment and development of our cultural identity as well as our sovereignty. Radio and television are the largest and most immediate distribution mechanisms for cultural products. I had hoped the Government would have provided increased funding for the CBC, the National Film Board, and Telefilm Canada for this purpose. These agencies are key to the development and strengthening of Canadian radio and television film production. The strengthening of these industries will become increasingly important as we forge closer commercial ties with the United States. Their success will depend on Telefilm Canada's reputation and stable funding.
Another aspect I had hoped to see addressed is with respect to a home for the National Archives of Canada, which is now in poor temporary quarters. It is short of space. Its archival holdings and its government records are at risk. These environmental conditions are not acceptable. We need to have a way in which to preserve our national heritage.
The standing committee has recommended that priority be given to the construction of a new facility which would meet the accommodation needs of the National Archives until the year 2010. It was the Minister's intention to move in that direction. I was disappointed to see that this was not found in the Budget or in the Minister's remarks.
In closing, I would like to quote Canadian publisher John MacFarlane who pointed out that it is important as a country to "make the distinction between importing merchandise and importing culture. Wearing foreign shoes and driving foreign cars won't make us any less Canadian, but without our own culture we're nothing more than a colony".
We cannot, it seems to me, preserve Canada's political sovereignty and cultural identity without protecting and developing our own cultural industries. They provide Canadian artists, creators and communicators with real and numerous opportunities for expressing and sharing their vision of Canada.
The closing ceremonies of the Olympics took place last evening. We all viewed its Canadian dimensions. Our Hockey Night in Canada and the Olympics are part of what make up the Canadian cultural milieu. I hope that we will give serious consideration to these matters as we look at the borrowing authority.

Member on the borrowing authority Bill which puts the country further in debt I was wondering if it is still the policy of the Liberal Party, and her policy as one who represents the riding of the former Prime Minister, to continue to borrow, borrow, borrow without end just because she has further demands and wants of the Government. It is as if we have a money tree out in the backyard from which we can pick further currency.
As the Hon. Member may, know there are further appropriations for culture in the budgetary figures handed down by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski). I wonder why the Member demands insistently for more borrowing. Does she want the Bill raised to $27 billion or $28 billion? Is $30 billion too little for her? Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member also had certain negative attitudes toward the capital cost allowance which was a way in which one could infuse risk dollars into the film industry. He did not care to support this measure to the degree I or the industry would have liked.
May I remind him that 60 per cent or more of the debt of the country has been accumulated under the management of his Government. If it would stop spending these incredible sums on nuclear submarines and put them where we need to place emphasis in Canada then we would be far better off. It is a matter of priorities. I find that the Government's priorities are not well directed.
If we accumulated a deficit in 1980, 1981 and 1982 1 remind the Hon. Member that the whole world was in a state of chaos and heading toward a depression. Canada did not have to put bread lines in place. But we now have bread lines, thanks to the management of his Government.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments. With regard to the Hon. Member's remarks, she takes a certain perverse delight in going about the country knocking Canadian arts and undermining Canadian culture. It is really a sad state of affairs when a Member of Parliament will not stand up in defence of Canadian arts, our artists and our creators.
This year in the Estimates $113 million has been added to the base budget of the Department of Communications and the portfolio. Some $53 million in additional resources will now be available to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There is a 5 per cent over-all increase in the envelope of the Department of Communications and the portfolio. This means additional increases for museums, broadcasting, the National Archives and a number of other fields.
What is important to note is that since that time we have added an additional $8 million to the Canada Council so that it can meet with requests from across the country that are
coming to it. We have also allocated $8 million for the expansion of the Art Gallery of Ontario. This is a tremendous project which serves Toronto, Ontario and, indeed, the whole of Canada.
Two years ago on a five-year basis we added an annual increase of $33 million to the production of feature films and dubbing and to a series for television. This amounts to a total of $165 million over this period of time.
We have added substantially to the budget of the sound recording industry. This has allowed a great increase in the number of Canadian songs performed by Canadian artists and recorded by Canadian recording companies.
These measures are taking place. At the end of the last calendar year newspaper after newspaper made comments such as, "This is the best year we have ever had in Canadian publishing". "This is the best year we have ever had in film production". "This is the best year we have ever had in Canadian sound recordings". Artists are reiterating that all across the country.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I suggest that the fine record that the Minister just read to Hon. Members has a great deal of substance to it. It is too bad that it was the previous Minister who brought in these measures and that this Minister has the worst record for interference and meddling in the cultural industries of any Minister in the history of the country.
I suggest that the Minister talk to representatives of the sound recording industry. She sent the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) to defend her stand. It was interesting to note that his observations on her behalf were not well received by the sound recording industry. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I have been looking forward for some time now to participating in today's debate, for a number of reasons not least of which is the fact that the Government is now asking permission of Parliament to borrow $25,300 million. 1 suspect that for most people it is difficult to get their minds around what $25,300 million is. It can best be described as a substantial sum of money. I do not think anyone can begin to even comprehend the thousands and thousands of millions of dollars that we are borrowing for a variety of purposes. I would say that one of the reasons is that the Government does not have its financial house in order.
I want to explain why I think the borrowing authority simply betrays the inability of the Government to come to grips with some of the real problems facing our country. In my estimation at the top of the list is the deficit. I do not think the
February 29, 1988

Government has dealt with the deficit adequately. I do not think the Government has taken the necessary steps to reduce the deficit. This will create an incredible amount of indebtedness for future generations of Canadians. The best thing that one could say is that the increasing, spiralling nature of the deficit of Canada has at least been capped. During the Liberal administration, we saw the deficit escalate almost to the stratosphere. It just got totally out of hand. It rose out of sight and beyond all comprehension.
Quite frankly, I think that Canadians in general and even people who do not follow the fiscal, financial and monetary policies of Government closely know that we are too heavily in debt. They know that the liability we are leaving future generations is quite frankly catastrophic. I do not think we have dealt satisfactorily with the deficit and 1 simply want to point out what I think were some missed opportunities. That is why we are now having to discuss giving the Government the support to borrow $25,300 million more.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Tories are always big spenders.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
As my friend has indicated, the Tories are big spenders. They like to buy votes in a sense. I know that that flies in the face of what many of my Conservative colleagues in the House of Commons have said over the years, but the facts speak for themselves.
Just recently, the Government tabled its expenditure plans for the forthcoming year. Right at the top of the list was a $2.5-billion slush fund. There were no programs earmarked for that $2.5 billion. To be fair, the Tories called it by a fancier name. They did not call it a pre-election slush fund. That would be a little too obvious, 1 suppose.
The Estimates clearly earmark $2.5 billion to be used to buy votes in various parts of Canada. The Government can expand an airport here, build a new port there, relocate a prison in some constituency there in the hopes of trying to buy the support of Canadians, sort of the hooker approach to politics. I do not think that that will work. 1 do not think Canadians will be bought off by the Government. Nevertheless, $2.5 billion has been earmarked for the next year for various projects that at this point have not been identified.
What does that tell us about the Government? Surely to goodness, if the Government has some vision of the future of this country, if it has been working closely with provincial, regional and local Governments, it should be able to predict now what these major projects worth $2.5 billion ought to be. If it cannot, then that is scandalous. Any Government that says it has no idea how it will spend $2.5 billion now but will have to determine that in the next few weeks and months is not the kind of Government Canada needs. We need a Government that has some vision of the future of Canada a Government that works with the other political jurisdictions at the
Borrowing Authority
regional and local levels to determine the appropriate initiatives the Government should be taking to ensure that economic prosperity returns to all parts of Canada, not simply pockets in southern Ontario. A Government that says it is concerned about the deficit but has a $2.5-billion slush fund is being very unrealistic in its expectation of support for this initiative.
I am concerned about another missed opportunity. If the Government were serious about deficit reduction, it ought to have dealt with the matter of interest-rate policy. We all recognize now that interest rates in the United States are lower than they are in Canada, particularly short-term interest rates. The argument that if we lower interest rates in Canada, there will be an exodus of money to the United States where the returns are better is absolute folly. Interest rates in the United States are much lower than they are in Canada.
1 say why not reduce interest rates by 1 per cent, 2 per cent or almost 3 per cent to get them down to the United States rates. Can you imagine, Madam Speaker, what it would mean to the deficit of Canada, to say nothing of the assistance it would give to small and medium-sized businesses and consumers, particularly in the regions? The cost of serving the unbelievable debt the Government has now given us, a debt of nearly $300 billion, would be significantly reduced if interest charges on the debt were reduced by 2 per cent. That is why I say that it was a missed opportunity. Not to have reduced interest rates to approximate those in the United States was a serious oversight by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Government of Canada. The deficit could have been reduced by another few billion dollars.
Another missed opportunity to reduce the deficit was tax reform or, as others have referred to it, tax deform. Tax deform is probably a more appropriate name for what the Minister of Finance has done to the tax system. The system remains unjust, unfair, discriminatory and biased in favour of the wealthy and the largest corporations rather than in favour of ordinary Canadians and medium and small-sized businesses.
You are probably filling out your tax return now, Madam Speaker. You have probably noticed that the tax return is no simpler than it was before. This notion of simplifying the tax system is absolute nonsense.
Over the weekend, I sat down for the first time to look at the tax return and the pages and pages of schedules. 1 do not know what on earth I will do. I think we ought to do what was done in the State of California. We ought to introduce legislation that requires Members of Parliament to fill out their own tax returns with no help from anyone. Then we would see some quick action.
I see that the Chairman of the Finance Committee knows full well that that is what should have been done. He is nodding. He knows full well that there was an opportunity to introduce a one-page or half-page tax return that would suffice for 75 per cent of Canadian citizens.

speechtext:
The Fraser Institute thinks it's a good idea.

February 29, 1988
Borrowing Authority

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Fraser Institute thinks it is a good idea. I think it is a good idea. I suspect most Canadians would revel at the thought of a one-page tax return for 75 per cent of the people. Why did we not do it? I think it is because we are trying to mystify the system. Still the Minister of Finance says that we have simplified the tax system. I cannot imagine a more nonsensical statement being made. I suppose if he says it loud enough and long enough, enough people will begin to believe that there must have been some improvement at least, though I cannot see any. Again, this was another missed opportunity.
Why on earth, when we had gone through months and months of discussion, did we not make the tax system fairer? Why on earth was the Minister of Finance required to rise in his place recently to announce that, in spite of all the Government's best efforts, there will still be 60,000 profitable corporations that will not pay a single penny in income tax next year? Of course, that is to say nothing of the tens of thousands of corporations that will pay $100 or $50.
I know that my friend, the Chairman of the Finance Committee, knows that the real tax rates of the big finance companies, the big trust companies, the big banks and most of the institutions in the financial community would probably average less than 3 per cent. How many Canadians enjoy a tax rate of about 3 per cent? Virtually none. I think it is disgraceful that the tax system allows so many profitable corporations, corporations with profits in excess of $200 million or $300 million per year, not to pay any income tax whatsoever, to say nothing of those that pay only a few dollars.
As 1 say, we are not talking about the mom and pop shop or the hair salon down the street. In 1986, for example, Alcan Aluminum made profits totalling $220 million. Not only did it not pay any income tax at all, it got a tax credit for next year of $32 million. Then there is the little company Brascan with profits totalling $187 million and a tax credit of $2.3 million.
1 will not take time to go through this long list of 60,000 profitable corporations that paid no income tax whatsoever, but I would point out that if the Government was serious about deficit reduction this was an opportunity to find new revenue amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. It did not do that. It said instead that it would allow these thousands of companies that make good profits every year to continue without paying any income tax whatsoever.
It is tragic when you think of it. Here was an opportunity, through changes to our interest rate policy and our tax system, to make the system more fair, equitable and just, but we did not do it. Instead, the Government created this big slush fund of money not earmarked for any particular project, to say nothing about a lot of peculiar spending by the Government.
In the coffee shops of Kamloops I still hear that people are outraged that they had to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars for Sinclair Stevens' legal bills. People are still outraged and ask why the Government had to give $5 million to help build the West Edmonton Mall for the Ghermezian brothers. They
did not need that money, but thousands of struggling small businesses did. That $5 million would have gone a long way for a lot of the small businesses in Alberta who are struggling to find some venture capital to establish a new product and get involved in a new creative business. They cannot get money from traditional lending institutions and could have used some of that $5 million.
There is a long list of ways that the Government decided to spend the taxpayers' money which I think people find very disappointing. I could also talk more about fiscal policy but I will move to some other areas because it has become clear that the Government is not serious in its efforts at deficit reduction. If it was, it would certainly have done things differently in the last number of months. Therefore, I want to spend the next few moments talking about the trade deal which the Government signed on January 2 with the United States of America.
A lot of people are asking what this deal will do to Canada. Is it a complete sell-out of our country to the U.S? Have we given away our economy to the U.S. multinational giants? What will it mean for jobs?
In spite of the statistics often presented to us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about how wonderfully Canada is doing, he forgets that while we are doing wonderfully in pockets of southern Ontario, such is not the case in most of the rest of Canada. In my Province of British Columbia, where unemployment in many communities is still in the 20 per cent to 30 per cent range, we have not noticed a tremendous improvement in the last four years of the Government's administration. In eastern Canada, where unemployment levels are as high as 40 per cent in some communities, they have not recognized any improvement, to say nothing about other parts of western Canada, northern Canada, or Quebec. It is not prosperity city in most of Canada today. Yes, indeed, in pockets of southern Ontario such is the case and we are pleased about that. However, we were looking in this most recent Budget and the Estimates for some real commitment to overcoming regional disparities.
Many of us are concerned that this trade deal will act against attempts by the federal Government to assist the regions. The American companies are going to be looking at these various programs to help our western farmers, East Coast fishermen and the forest industry throughout the regions and calling them subsidies producing unfair competition. The fact that they have the same kind of subsidies back home is irrelevant to them. All they have to do is prove there is some unfair subsidy here.
We saw this just the other day with the flow-through shares issue. The U.S. said if the federal Government, through the tax system, provides encouragement for the mining sector to explore for minerals, that is unfair. What did the Government do? It gutted the program and made it very difficult for exploration companies to raise capital to carry on their activities. This is critical, as you well know, because without that upstream investment, nothing will happen.
February 29, 1988

As you know, this exploration is usually done by small and medium-sized Canadian companies. Much of the mining operations might be done by larger companies, in some cases multinationals, but in this case we are talking almost exclusively, 100 per cent, about Canadian-owned companies out there in the trenches, in the hinterlands, exploring for new mineralization. Flow-through shares was a way in which the federal Government could encourage and support those junior Canadian companies. Now it has decided to gut the program but what is it going to replace it with?
To be fair, particularly to my friend, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, this is not the only way to assist mining exploration and show that we support their initiative. There are other more direct ways of support, if you like. However, the Government is apparently not going to do anything, just hang these small companies out to dry at a very critical time.
To go back for a moment to the trade initiative, what does it mean with respect to jobs? We have to look to the evidence to arrive at an answer. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), an honest man, one with integrity, a man who likes to tell it like it is, when he was asked how many jobs this trade deal might cost Canadians, had the courage to say it could be as high as 500,000. His predecessor and other cabinet Members have used figures as high as 800,000. There is no question there are going to be major adjustments. The royal commission which took a number of years to look into the whole matter of what they call free trade, which of course this deal is not, said it would cost the federal Government up to $5 billion in adjustment costs because of the tremendous dislocation that will occur in our economy. That means a lot of people are going to lose their jobs.
On the one hand we hear the Minister saying it could be as many as 500,000 jobs. Then we look at the work that the Department of Finance has done and we see that the best case scenario is that over five years it could create 125,000 jobs. That is 25,000 jobs a year. Yet in a good month, when our productivity is doing well, we can create that many jobs alone.
You have indicated my time is up. 1 just got started on this dissertation but unfortunately the rules prohibit me from continuing. Therefore, in closing, with respect to a serious situation facing this country, that being the deficit, unfortunately the most recent initiatives taken by the Government have eliminated those initiatives which could have helped reduce the deficit.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the House Leader of the New Democratic Party some questions. 1 was quite interested in his desire to become associated with the Fraser Institute in terms of simplified tax returns.
Borrowing Authority
Has he had an opportunity to discuss with his colleague, the finance critic for his Party, the recent trip of the Finance Committee to New Zealand where, as he will know, a socialist labour government is in power? Has he discussed with his colleagues how that socialist labour government was in the process of selling out their national oil company to a British multinational?
Does he think we should do as they did and cancel all farm subsidies, lower farm interest rates, and all assistance to farmers completely as they did? Does he think that in order to squeeze inflation out of the system we ought to raise interest rates to 19 per cent as they have?
Does he think that in order to get the tax system down to a flat tax system we ought to disallow any contributions to pension plans or registered retirement savings plans as a deduction against taxable income?
Finally, on a sales tax issue, would he be supportive of taxes on food and even taxes on municipal taxes in order to keep the system simple?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my hon. friend's intervention because I did forget one very important item in my presentation and this will allow me to refer to it briefly, that is, the decision of the federal Government to impose a national sales tax on all Canadians. It will make interesting election campaigning when Conservative candidates are promising changes to the tax system which will result in new taxes on everyone for virtually every business transaction with the exception of the purchase of food, as the Minister of Finance has indicated.
I appreciate that the Minister listened to the consumers of Canada who said that a tax on food and prescription drugs would be unethical and, quite frankly, unacceptable to the people of Canada, which point was raised by our finance critic on so many occasions that it became boring.
1 am not familiar with what efforts are being undertaken in every country of the world to come to grips with the challenges facing them. However, 1 am aware of what is going on in our country. I am aware of the Government's decision to cut back on support for the mining industry. This fits into an over-all program. As I see it, the Government has a program in place to depopulate rural Canada. It has not been very explicit or articulate about the program but it is a program to pull support from small communities and rural Canada.
The Post Office is the most obvious vehicle of this initiative. The Government's plan is to cut back postal services in rural Canada. In my own constituency in the last month the Government has attempted to close two post offices. We are trying to fight that. However, it is very clear that the Government has made a decision to use this method to encourage people to move into the big cities. I do not think that is right or appropriate.

February 29, 1988
Borrowing Authority
My colleague mentioned my support for the initiative of the Fraser Institute to simplify our tax returns. You bet, Madam Speaker, I see no reason why we must have the complicated, convoluted tax system which we do have in terms of the returns which people must fill out. There is no reason for it. The Member, who is the Chairman of the Finance Committee, will know that work had been done on a one-page tax return which would have been sufficient for the vast majority of Canadian citizens. People are subjected to trauma in their efforts to determine how much tax they owe or how much tax they have already paid the Government in hopes of a small refund. This ought not take place in the case of most Canadians. This is one page out of the many volumes of the Fraser Institute which I would have to support. I do not support many of their pages, but this would certainly be one which I do support.
With regard to the Member's points on initiatives taken by the Government in New Zealand, 1 am afraid that I am not equipped at this time to comment intelligently on those.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Member opposite brings to our attention that his riding is being depopulated. I presume the people are going to the cities for jobs. If the people of his riding were to get a little wiser and elect a Conservative Member who believes in job creation in the private sector and economic opportunity, perhaps people would stay in the riding.
I simply offer that as a suggestion. We would be happy to see a conversion and have him come across the floor.
The Member's speech, in a somewhat uncharacteristic way, contained a lot of sophistry. I want the people who are watching to recall and perhaps read in Hansard what the Member said about the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) with regard to 500,000 or 800,000 jobs. The Member attempted to leave the impression that that would produce 500,000 or 800,000 unemployed Canadians. Those numbers are used in reference to the capacity of the free trade deal to bring about adjustments in the Canadian economy so that people will have better jobs in the future than they have today. They will have higher paid and more highly skilled jobs.
The Member started with the figure of $10 billion and then said that it would cost the taxpayers $5 billion for adjustment. He left the impression that these would be unemployed people. The purpose of adjustment funds, be it $5 billion, $10 billion, or $20 billion, is for ordinary Canadians to attain increased skills and increased job opportunities with better working conditions and higher salaries.
The absolute minimum economic analysis is that the first five years of the trade deal will produce 125,000 additional jobs. That is the critical part which the Member very cleverly slides over. We are not talking about creating 25,000 jobs a year in Canada. The Government's economic policy is producing more than 30,000 jobs a month and has been doing so for three and a half years. How do we get 1.25 million more Canadians employed than were employed three and a half years ago unless we are producing jobs at that rate? The free trade deal will produce an additional 125,000 jobs. People now on the unemployment rolls will have jobs. It will produce
better quality jobs for Canadians and the adjustment fund will ensure that that happens.
I suspect that the Member was in a conflict of interest with the reality that labour union leaders provide so much of the funding for the New Democratic Party and have a desire to protect the jobs which they already have in their unions. They have no commitment to the total Canadian mosaic and the twelve and a half million people employed in Canada but are trying to do that which they were elected to do, protect the selfish interests of the members of that particular union.
That is what unions are about. They do that very well and are useful in Canadian society, but it is a tragedy that a political party in the Chamber is so clearly a captive of that single mentality on behalf of this very privileged group which controls the supply of labour and fights very hard on behalf of its members. However, the total Canadian society will be well served by the free trade deal.
We are on the borrowing Bill and perhaps the Hon. Member would like to tell us what justification he has for the use of tax credits? He brought up the issue of tax credits. Everyone who donates to a political Party receives a tax credit so taxpayers pay part of the contribution to the Party. What justification does the Hon. Member have for giving free trips to socialist countries. That is one of the things the New Democratic Party is doing. What justification does he have for the tendency to take campaign expenses and move them over to the column called "election expenses", receiving a larger rebate from the taxpayers of Canada, to fund the Party on the longer term?
If the Hon. Member is concerned about tax credits that are devoted to the creation of jobs for ordinary Canadians, how much concern does he have about the use of the tax credit system by his own political Party to service its political ends?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a long list of inaccuracies presented by the Hon. Member. I do not know where to begin. February 29, 1988

In closing, I simply want to say that there is much yet to do,
I found it of some interest that the Government, looking for new ideas, new suggestions and new ways of doing things with respect to a change in our tax system, went to the socialist country of New Zealand to seek out better ways and means of changing our tax system and government economic development policy.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the spirit of this Chamber, of being able to provide a proper exchange of views, 1 would like to begin by looking at the assertions made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Hawkes) who is a well known expert in the art of sophistry. He was commenting on the views of my colleague. It is certainly well known within the boundaries of this House that if there was ever a practitioner of that particular art, the Parliamentary Secretary deserves the full accolades of this House.
The Parliamentary Secretary talks about the so-called economic benefits of the proposed trade arrangement. Let us examine what those are on the basis of the Government's documents, not some of the other analyses or studies. Let us look at what the Government says. The Department of Finance produced its own document trying to put the best face possible on the trade arrangement. One would have assumed that the promises and expectations held out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), that there will be this incredible gravy train of growth and jobs sort of sloshing over the country, would have been confirmed in the figures. However, instead we received a projection of an incremental growth rate of one-half of 1 per cent per year. That is so marginal, so meaningless, that in terms of computer forecasting, no analyst worth his salt would not even take that into account and provide it as a legitimate proposition. It simply does not add up. When our own growth rate varies, depending on the time of year, between 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent and 4 per cent in a good year, to say that we expect, on the best possible scenario, a growth rate of one-half of 1 per cent is hardly going to provide comfort and solace to all those who will be losing their jobs.
Of course, what the study also predicted was that the jobs will come only through increased consumer spending, primarily in the service sector. It is also well known that that is the lowest paying sector of the economy. It is a sector where there are far higher incidents of temporary and part-time work. The question of what the service sector will do under free trade has never been studied, itself. So we are really flying blind. We are being asked to accept a set of economic forecasts in which the analysis has not been done, and the large macro studies have a marginal Mickey Mouse interpretation to them.
That study, that was highly cited by the Parliamentary Secretary, did not include the increased tax costs the Canadian people will have to bear. They will have to pay $450 million in the next year, an extra cent on every litre of gas they buy, adding up to a $2 billion additional tax grab in the fifth year of the agreement. That was not put into the computation, nor was
Borrowing Authority
the question of additional adjustment costs that someone will have to pay. We know the stingy federal Government is not going to pay them, so that means it will fall upon the private sector or the provincial Governments to pay.
It is even more ironic when the Government talks about the new jobs and new skills training when in fact its own job strategy is in absolute shambles. It is in total disarray. The community colleges across Canada are having to close down their courses because they are not receiving sufficient funding. The money that is supposed to be going for training in the private sector is not being monitored, so that the money can be used to train someone to push a broom, instead of to train them on the computer. No one knows because they are not being monitored properly.
There is no money to deal with the problem of illiteracy, to bring Canadians who have low job skills and lack of basic English and mathematics to the point where they can get into a training position, because the Canadian Jobs Strategy has cancelled all these programs. The Canadian Jobs Strategy has abandoned hundreds of thousands of Canadians, forcing cancellation of community college programs, supporting unmonitored, unevaluated programs in the private sector where the quality of training is questionable. Yet the Parliamentary Secretary has the nerve to say, "We are going to be training skilled workers for the future". The National Training Act, which was one of the best training programs in the world, has been turned into one of the worst, all in a matter of three and one-half years. That is a great accomplishment.
I challenge any Conservative Member of Parliament to stand up and argue the case for the Canadian Job Strategy, to put facts and figures on the table as to what it is doing. They can challenge what 1 have just said if they think it is wrong, but I have the evidence right here as to how it is working. I have taken some time to study it, something I am sure Tory Members have not because they refuse to face that kind of calamity.
In the Province of Manitoba, in the next year alone, the amount of money going into job training and Jobs employment will go from $75 million to $48 million, an almost 30 per cent cut in one year.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Look at the results, though.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Some unknown voice opposite tells me to look at the results. I can tell him the results in terms of some of the private business sectors where they are training people to push a broom. I met last weekend with people at Rossbrook House, which used to have training programs for young native kids so they could get into the job force, and those programs have been cancelled. Those are the results. I tell the Hon. Member that it is a national tragedy what the Government is perpetrating upon Canadians. If it had any guts or courage it would start admitting it and change the program or throw the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) out of his job. He is not only fumbling on the immigration side but he is fumbling badly on the job creation and employment side.

February 29, 1988
Borrowing Authority
It is terrible what is going on. The Government says, "Oh, we are going to prepare for the bright new future. We will have highly skilled Canadians", but we have a job training program which is in shambles, where the whole foundation is dissolving around us. Yet the Government tries to defend that kind of program.
Another area where sophistry has become the order of the day as opposed to results is in the area of regional development. I could think of no more important priority for a federal government than to ensure equity in the country. Because of our geography and the nature of the population being spread across 8,000 kilometres and a large northern span of territory, a primary responsibility of any federal government is to ensure that people are treated the same, that there is a sense of equality and fairness. The expectation should be that the federal Government will have standards in which all receive a fair meting out of resources.
In the early 1980s we brought in a new economic regional development program. It was designed to work in co-operation with the provinces. We would sit down and work out priorities with each of the provinces and then use federal funds to invest in those regions. It was not based solely on indexes of poverty, but also on what would be the primary focal points of growth and development, region by region.
In my own region we sat down with the provincial Government and the City of Winnipeg, invested in downtown development where we felt that the improvement and enhancement of the urban environment would be a major incentive to private capital investment. For an investment of $30 million in the north of Portage, the result has been that we generated $450 million of additional private capital. That is good leverage by any judgment; the major renewal of the downtown area.
We sat down with the province and felt that transportation would be a major focal point of growth. It is the largest supplier of jobs in my home province. We began to invest in the infrastructure, development of the Port of Churchill, new research facilities at the university, proposed new maintenance base for VIA Rail, a computer centre for CNR, the development of new hopper cars to deal with the prairie grain trade in the Transcona Shops, and improvement of the airports to provide for international trade.
We also concentrated on the cultural communications area, in an attempt to build up in the City of Winnipeg and the Province of Manitoba an increased capacity for growth in the cultural areas. We then added supplementary programs in agriculture and minerals. All of those were designed in full cooperation with the Province of Manitoba and with the municipalities and the groups involved.
Those agreements were signed and they amounted to half a billion dollars' worth. I am not saying that they were perfect, but it was the beginning of a co-operative approach to economic development, and an attempt to bring all the parties together to ensure that the federal Government was a major player on plans that were developed and blueprints organized in the local region.
After the 1984 election what happened? The new Government cancelled many of the transportation projects. It cancelled the development of the major robotic research centre which would have given the country, not only western Canada, a major, first-class, world-class research centre for robotic technology. In this area we lag far behind. The Japanese out-gun us 10 to 1 in the development of robotic technology, but we cancelled a research centre which would have provided the private sector with an inducement or incentive to develop in that area.
In the Port of Churchill there was a slow-down. The projects are still waiting to be funded. There was cancellation of a major renewable energy resource corporation. We also had the famous incident of the CF-18, and withdrawal of that major opportunity for western Canada to get into the new frontiers of the aerospace business. Those actions were undertaken unilaterally, without consultation, and in contradiction to the economic development plans that had already been developed.
That runs against the spirit of federalism. It also shows that there is no economic development priority based upon equity or fairness. We are now told that there will be a new Western Diversification Fund. In looking at the estimates of that and the projects, what do we find? Of the projects already announced, not one includes any major project in the Province of Manitoba.
Is that because the Province of Manitoba does not support the Government on its trade proposals? Is it because it has an NDP Government? Whatever the reason, how does one explain a pattern where there was very clear, very significant co-operation between federal-provincial governments in 1984, and since 1984 nothing but warfare, confrontation, withdrawal and subtraction of federal assistance?
Is that what one would call a fair system? Is that what one would call a system in which the federal government is seen to be an equal provider of its own investment? Is that seen as a way of ensuring that one million people who live in a significant province in this country in terms of opportunities that it can provide are being totally ignored by the Government? Does it suggest a weakness around the Cabinet table of the Manitoba representatives? Does it simply say that one of the provinces of Canada is being frozen out, is deliberately and politically being isolated? That is what I suggest is the reason.
February 29, 1988

When we are asked to talk about a borrowing authority, one goes on the basis that there will be some level of fairness applied to it. If the Manitoba taxpayers are asked to support further expenditures by their own Government in Canada, one would assume and expect that perhaps they would want some return and that they would feel they were part of the system and going to be calculated in in the same way.
In the last two or three weeks, what do we find? In total contradiction to a signed agreement, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is breaking that agreement by withdrawal of 300 senior employees in the CN headquarters in western Canada, particularly in Winnipeg. The agreement itself clearly states that the Crown corporations of Canada involved in the field of transportation will make every effort to enhance and augment their employment and their research and development. This Government is acknowledging its withdrawal.
Let us look at a very crucial area of rail line improvement. One of the most important areas that we have known in western Canada to maintain our smaller communities is the maintenance of the rail line network. In 1984 when I was Minister of Transport we signed a major agreement with the railroads which required that each year they would follow a clear program of rehabilitation. This is the last year of the program, and the Minister of Transport is committing $25 million, leaving $125 million still in the bag.
Do you know how many communities that will affect, Madam Speaker, how many smaller places in western Canada will find that they will no longer have a rail line in two or three years?
I find it difficult to believe that a Government that states that it wants national reconciliation, which in 1984 based its election mandate on there being an end to confrontation, is engaging in the very same and more extreme forms of antifederal initiatives. It is clearly discriminating against certain provinces of this country. It is withdrawing federal presence, federal investment, and federal activity. That has connotations and repercussions far beyond the immediate area of economic growth or jobs. It will weaken the linkages of this country. It will undermine the connecting links across Canada in a very fundamental manner.
Let us look at what disturbs those of us from western Canada who are Members of Parliament. When we look at political surveys from that part of the country-and they may not be printed in the central Canadian or eastern press-we see western Canadians being asked whether they would support a legitimate western Party and some 30 per cent to 40 per cent saying that they would. The reason is that in the last three or four years, rather than foster a greater sense of participation in Canada, the Government has succeeded in pushing western Canadians further away with the kinds of actions that I have outlined so far.
Borrowing Authority
This brings me back to the topic with which I opened, that is, the proposed trade agreement. There is an implicit assumption that somehow-and I think the Prime Minister spoke about it in Calgary before Christmas-this will be a bonanza for western Canada, when in fact the hard figures show no such thing. In fact, a number of very essential western Canadian industries will be put in jeopardy. The food processing industry, one of the largest industries in my own province, will be forced to shut down, or the supply management system will be forced to shut down. This is the dilemma faced by the Campbell Soups, the McCains, and the other major food processors in my province. That could be repeated for many of the smaller industries. The trade agreement will not mean alternate growth; in many cases it will pull away the growth. However, the Parliamentary Secretary says that we do not need adjustment or any help for the workers and communities affected, that it will take care of itself in the market-place.
We in western Canada know better. We know that the way to develop is through a partnership of the public and private sectors. It is a partnership which has made western Canada grow, and the Government is withdrawing from that partnership. For that reason this request for a borrowing authority is really the height of sophistry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite said that I said that we would not need adjustment. I have never said that in my life, nor would I ever say it. The labour force constantly needs adjustment, and when we have a major positive initiative, such as free trade, we will need more adjustment than at other times. I very much resent people trying to put words in my mouth that 1 have never uttered. I want to make crystal clear that the pattern of the Hon. Member opposite in doing that kind of thing is well known in the House, but perhaps not well known to Canadians, so I simply wanted to point it out to them.
He began with an attack on the Canadian Jobs Strategy, which took a great deal of courage from that particular Hon. Member. Canadians may have forgotten the Liberal approach to unemployment problems in Canada. I stood in the House, when he was Minister and I was critic on the other side, and asked repeatedly in Question Period for an explanation of why a Liberal cabinet Minister would be receiving government employment creation grants which averaged out at $586 for every unemployed person in his or her riding, while unemployed people in my riding of Calgary West received employment creation funds at the rate of $12 per unemployed person.
It was a policy approach, his policy approach, that consistently created first-class unemployed Canadians and second-class unemployed Canadians. Year after year there was no fairness to the system. This unfairness was clearest in western Canada, and he was the Minister for western Canada. He talked about adjustment. Well, the National Energy Program was a program that required adjustment in my region. We moved from a 4 per cent unemployment rate to 13 per cent and

February 29, 1988
Borrowing Authority
14 per cent unemployment rates. That was the adjustment. They took 4 per cent unemployment and made it into 13 per cent or 14 per cent unemployment through one simple policy initiative which he supported and promoted. It threw people out of work. We must couple that with the use of employment creation grants of $12 per year per unemployed person. They create the problem, and then they take the money and put it in another part of the country, not where the unemployment was created. That is the Liberal idea of adjustment.
Let us refer to what our Government did. I see the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) is here. She replaced that Hon. Member as Minister of Employment and Immigration and very quickly looked at the 50 some odd programs which he had created to parcel money to Liberal partisans and constituency organizations. One had to be a Liberal to get help under that Government. It was not enough to be a Canadian; one had to be a Liberal Canadian. Our Minister reduced them down to six programs. She restored some sense of local choice in terms of local unemployed people and local labour markets. She devoted all the money, not to partisans of a political Party but to the recipients to help them gain more skills, and started working on the adjustment concern right from the start of the life of this Government. With all that money that was parcelled out for cleaning river banks, or doing things which sometimes did not even exist-la table de pique-nique dans la province de Quebec-we must never forget the Liberal approach to this problem. It has been replaced by an educational approach. Taxpayers' dollars go to individuals to help them gain more skills for their future, and if their future as Canadians improves, the country's economy improves. It is working.
The unemployment rate for young people, the most difficult group, in three short years has dropped from nearly 19 per cent to 12 per cent. We have solved one-third of the problem in three years, and if we get four more years we will halve the problem. That is what will happen, because we have a philosophy of investing in Canadians, taking the skills and drives which already exist, and helping them to improve their skills and to retain the drive to succeed. When individual Canadians work together to look at economic opportunities and to be productive, the economy improves and improves. It is a combination of policies which has provided those one million, one hundred and some odd thousand Canadians with jobs today who did not have jobs three years ago.
The Hon. Member talked about hard figures. The hard evidence is the capacity of Canadians to produce, to sell, and to prosper if government stays out of their road and provides assistance in the background where needed.
I simply say to the Hon. Member opposite that Canadians do not want the Liberal approach to employment creation where one must be a Liberal to get money. They want a fair program for all Canadians dedicated to the adjustment skills issue.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member talks about what Canadians want. I just cite the recent poll in the Province of Manitoba where we are 14 points ahead of the Tory Party federally. It seems to me that they know what they want an awful lot more than what the Hon. Member seems to know. I would only remind him that they know what happens when they have a Liberal Government. They know how federal investment can be used to generate growth.
Let me give the Hon. Member an example. I am glad that he is practising to be the employment and immigration critic again, because he will have to employ those skills in a very short time. Let me tell him about something that happened last Friday. I visited a place called Rossbrook House, a drop-in centre for young people. It primarily services native youth and is located in the downtown area of Winnipeg. It is run by a group of Catholic nuns. They were recipients of community employment programs when I was Minister. They used those programs to hire young native kids who did not have any job skills and who had left school in grade seven or eight. They brought them into the job market and gave them some employment as counsellors. This enabled them to develop some rudimentary skills. This was used as a way to develop a transition between that and going on to future training.
Under the vaunted Canadian Jobs Strategy, about which the Hon. Member talks, there are not those programs any longer. They have been cut off. The group of young Canadians about which he talked are being told that they do not rate anymore. That is an example of what is being duplicated right across the country. If one is in a low income bracket, out of the market or suffers from illiteracy then the Government does not care. Its jobs strategy is not designed for this person.
I would now like to deal with the fact that we are short of several thousand job training places in the western Canadian provinces because under the vaunted Canadian Jobs Strategy the Government has not put money into this area. It has not created a single new training space in the country. Under the Canadian Skills Growth Program we were investing in the community colleges, including those in the province of the Hon. Member, to provide new spaces, new equipment and new opportunities. The Canadian Jobs Strategy does not provide any investment of that type whatsoever.
Let us talk about the question of the special needs groups in our society. There is no doubt that one of the important reasons for our job creation programs was to support the social service system of the country since it was being clobbered by provincial Governments and municipal Governments. They could not afford the extra programs to provide the extra services to battered women, displaced kids or homeless families. Our job creation programs went to those groups directly so that they could hire people and provide services. Those programs have been cut off. They have been withdrawn.
February 29, 1988

Is the Hon. Member saying that, yes, the strategy is designed to support the friends of the Government in the business community who are receiving all types of grants which are not being monitored or evaluated and which are certainly not being used for training? They are being used as a way of subsidy back into some of those businesses. The quality of the training is so pathetic that it makes one weep.
That is the Tory way of doing it. That is fine. I am glad that that is the approach that they take. I think that Canadians know that there is an alternative. There is the skilful use of the public sector.
It is interesting to note that in the provinces of western Canada, about which the Hon. Member talked, in 1987-88 in Manitoba in particular job funds dropped from $75 million to $48 million. In Saskatchewan the funds went from $58 million down to $39 million. Even in the Province of Alberta the figure went from $141 million down to $103 million. Who is talking about increases when those provinces are experiencing cuts of 30 per cent? I think that the Hon. Member had better start to look at the Estimates of the Department of Employment to find out who is trying to serve the people of western Canada. He might start to look at the figures rather than to continue on in the fantasy in which he lives perpetually.

speechtext: The period provided for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse).

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am surprised that none of the government Members wish to defend their application to the House for some $25,300 million. Perhaps the proposition is so hard to defend that they find it easier to sit in their seats.
These funds apparently are to be used, as the Bill states, as may be required for public works and general purposes and shall expire March 31, 1989, to the extent that the unused authority exceeds $3 billion. In other words, once again we will carry into the next fiscal year some $3 billion. This means that something in the order of $28,300 million or thereabouts is being carried by the Government as a borrowing authority. We presume that this will be used basically to cover the deficit that is being projected at slightly higher than that amount of money.
This is the type of measure that a great many small businesses and farmers undertake at the beginning of every year. They go into the bank to obtain a lending authority from the bank. They establish a line of credit. Essentially, that is what the Government is attempting to do with this particular Bill. It is attempting to get that authority from the House of Commons, the body which is supposed to monitor Government expenditures and without whose consent Government could not spend the money. The Government comes to us and asks for the right to borrow money to the extent that I have just noted when tax revenues fall short of meeting the current expenditures.
Borrowing Authority
Habitually, we find that there is usually a big lending authority requested early in the year, as is this one, and then there will be a series of smaller ones made later on. We will not know until later on just how large the next series of expenditures will be. However, I do note that in reviewing the Estimates for 1988-89 that expenditures will continue to climb. In the fiscal year that we are about to finish I note that budgetary expenditures went up 7.7 per cent at a time when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was telling us how carefully he had reduced expenditures and how he had control of the Budget and how he had the deficit in hand.
In going through the Budget papers that were presented a couple of weeks ago, I wanted to find out just how much in hand this budgetary deficit was. I found that it is not quite as well in hand as the Minister leads us to believe.
When he became Minister of Finance in mid-1984-85 we had a gross accumulated deficit of about $200 billion, according to the papers that he presented with his Budget. It is listed as $199,092 million. Today, in the 1986-87 year, we have a net public debt of $264 billion. This means that in the period of time that the Minister of Finance has been in charge of the finances of the country the deficit has increased more than 30 percentage points. In fact, more than 30 per cent of the accumulated debt of the country since 1867 has been accumulated in the three and one-half years that the Minister has been the Minister of Finance. He says that we have the deficit in hand. He says that he is staying the course. He leaves the impression that the course is to get us out of debt and to get the public finances in some order.
I mentioned the extra billions of dollars, some $165 billion, that he has left future generations to carry. Some people say that it does not really matter. They say that what is really important is how large the deficit is in relation to the Gross National Product. So let us look at how he has managed under that set of rules.
When he became the Minister of Finance we had just shifted from 39.6 per cent of our national debt to Gross National Product. In other words our national debt was accumulated debt and equalled 39.6 per cent of that year's Gross National Product. At the end of 1986-87, which is included in the Budget papers, we find that our net public debt accumulated over all the years is now 51.8 per cent of our Gross National Product instead of the 39.6 per cent. I am afraid that staying the course will not solve the problem the Minister has defined as being one of the main problems the country faces.
We note that the Government has reduced the Public Service by a considerable amount. There are many fewer employees now than there were before, yet expenditures have not dropped as a result of this tactic. The first Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had budgetary expenditures in the neighbourhood of $111 billion. This year's expenditures are expected to be $132.25 billion, some 20 per cent higher than they were when this Minister became the Minister of Finance.

February 29, 1988
Borrowing Authority
Staying the course has not really changed the direction taken by previous administrations. Expenditure are still up and they are rising more rapidly than inflation. In fact, last year the forecasted percentage increase in expenditures was 7.7 per cent while inflation was at about 4.7 per cent or 4.8 per cent. This Minister who was so critical of previous expenditure programs is continuing to follow the same route as the much-maligned Liberals who preceded him.
1 would like to comment on some of the Government's expenditure policies which affect western Canadians and farmers across Canada. Other speakers have noted the job-creation plans of the Government. I wonder if there were plans. How can there be plans for job creation by a Government that claims to be opting out of all economic activity and leaving it to the private sector? I do not understand that, but perhaps the argument that is being made is that the private sector, thanks to being unleashed through less onerous taxes, has created jobs. I suppose that is the rationale the Minister is proposing to use for the job creation of which he boasts.
I note that most of the jobs that have been created have in fact been created in the Province of Ontario and most of those in the vicinity of Toronto, a very hot market at the moment. Those in the regions where most of the farmers for whom I speak live have not noticed that things have improved greatly.
Those who incurred debts during the time when interest rates were very high have not seen interest rates drop markedly under this Government. In fact, over the last six or eight months they have risen. This past year they were 1 per cent to 1.25 per cent higher than they were before. The farmers and small business people who make up most of the population of my riding are finding things actually worse than they were a year ago at Budget time.
A great many of the producers in my riding are in the export business. They export grain, beef, pork and light farm machinery. They find that the amount of money they receive for their product is down as well. At the same time as the Government has allegedly been fighting high interest rates by allowing them to rise another 1.25 per cent, it has also permitted the dollar to float higher.
Last year at Budget time the dollar was worth 72 or 73 cents. It is now floating at around 78 or 79 cents. This is bad news for the export industries in my riding. It means that they receive about 10 to 12 per cent less from their exports, in American dollars which are now bringing in fewer Canadian dollars. The Government's policies on interest rates and the dollar have not been good for the farmers and small businessmen of my riding.
Those people who have had problems carrying old debts have been attempting to refinance through the Farm Credit Corporation. They have found that it is even more difficult to get an FCC loan than ever before. The amount of business FCC has generated over the past year is down considerably. The Government has instructed the corporation to limit loans
to the amount of repayments. In other words, it is not proposing to give the FCC any new money. The only money it has to loan out is money from recycled loans that were paid off.
The interest rates that the Government has insisted the FCC use have been so high that very few people have used the services of the corporation. It has actually built up a small surplus of repayments over new loans. FCC interest rates rose a few months ago from 11.75 per cent on long-term loans to 12.25 per cent at this time. This was in the face of a policy goal presented to the corporation at a federal-provincial conference some time ago of having long-term credit rates to farmers at 9 per cent. After setting that goal, interest rates went from 11.75 per cent up to 12.25, not exactly a move toward the goal.
I note that the rail line rehabilitation program is away behind schedule. The program is due to end at the end of this year. Hon. Members know that some $125 million should have been expended in previous years on that program but that money is still left uncommitted. In fact, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) apparently has no intention of committing those funds to comply with the agreement that was supposed to exist between the people in my part of the country and the Government of Canada to bring branch lines up to permanent standards so farmers could move their products to market.
There seems to be a real distaste on the part of the Government to complete its commitment. There are a number of lines in my own riding which very clearly meet the criteria. Lines are ranked on the basis of cost-to-benefit, and the ones that would provide the most benefit to the whole economy, not just locally, at the least cost are the ones that meet the criteria. However, some of those lines which meet the criteria are having difficulty getting funds. Civil servants have clearly stated that those are priority lines and have ranked them accordingly, but the final decision which is made at the ministerial level has been delayed, and why there should be disputes from the Ministers, I do not know.
We find these decisions delayed because the Ministers involved apparently have some plans for the funds to go to other lines which happen to be in ridings held by very prominent members of the Government side. However, the return ratio of these lines is less than half of that of the lines that have been designated priority by the civil servants, some of which are in my riding.
I find it very strange that the Government would not move to improve the high-priority lines. If the lines were improved, costs to the producers in the area would be reduced. It would reduce costs by freeing up more than 500 hopper cars annually. That is the extra number of cars that will be available to the whole system if these lines are upgraded. Yet the Government has been dragging its feet on the matter. Instead of putting in the funds it talks about freedom to move and all the benefits that can accrue to a local community and economy if there is freedom of choice, to use the Government's words.
February 29, 1988

The Government seems to think this will somehow be a job-creating kind of scheme. I suppose it would be if it did not upgrade the line which of itself would be a job-creating scheme. Some Conservatives seem to think if they do not upgrade these lines what we will have instead is a lot of local employment with truckers moving grain 30 and 40 miles to the new railway points. This will employ more people driving trucks and maintaining and building roads. Unfortunately, it will also create a much higher cost system for local farmers and local communities. They will have to pay higher local taxes to maintain the road system. Local farmers will have to pay more for getting the grain trucked to the railway. It is a very shoddy type of economics and the worst kind of attempted political patronage 1 think I have witnessed in my eight years in politics. Yet this seems to be the direction the Conservatives wish to take this country.
Perhaps it also explains the manipulation of expenditures, with an attempt to create jobs, and may also explain why we have forecasted increases in expenditures in the last two years of the mandate of some 7.7 per cent and 5.5 per cent, while at the beginning of the mandate the actual increase in expenditures was 1.9 per cent. The Minister attempted to establish his credibility as a cost cutter in the first years. While he still believes in laying off the Public Service he continues to spend more money. 1 think that is in part caused by replacing civil servants with contracts to private corporations or individuals who in fact provide the same service at higher cost.
That seems to be the case with respect to public research, particularly in the Department of Agriculture. Since the Government took over there has been a cut-back of some 500 person-years in the research capacity of that department. Many of those positions are for professionals, some are technicians and other back-up services.
This I suppose represents the philosophical approach the current Government seems to have that research should be conducted by private rather than public entities. I think that is a grave mistake. I know of a number of instances where public research has resulted in great savings for individual farmers and consumers. This kind of research would never be conducted by private firms because there would be no reason to engage in research that would find ways of avoiding buying their products, for example. I think public research has to continue. It has a very good role to play and I hope the expenditures in future Budgets take that into account.
I see you are signalling that my time is up. I will close by remarking that I find it very difficult to understand how we can continue to have these very high debt loads going into our fiscal year, $25.3 billion being borrowed up front, knowing we will have to come back to the House for more, at a time when the Minister says he is reducing the deficit. Yet, as I pointed
Borrowing Authority
out, it has gone up phenomenally during the course of this Minister's tenure in office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have listened with great interest to the Hon. Member opposite. I have two very critical questions to ask him.
He was not in the House, nor was I, during the last minority Government of 1972, 1973, and 1974. However, we know that the current Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was then the Minister of Finance. As such he raised expenditures in two successive budget years by 30 per cent and more. His Government put in place policies that reduced the growth of income. The debt problems we are talking about today are a direct consequence of the NDP support for that minority Liberal Government which tried to bribe the voters through increased expenditures without any sense of fiscal responsibility concerning raising offsetting revenue.
My first question is this. If faced with a similar situation in the future, will he and his Party behave in the same way? His Party argued consistently for spending and we hear very little about revenue raising. He did not mention in his speech that the recent Budget would require no borrowing, we would not be standing in this House today asking to borrow $25.3 billion if we did not have to pay interest on money borrowed because of policies supported by the NDP in partnership, as usual, with the Liberal Party. We would have a surplus of well over $3 billion this year which we could use to reduce the debt Canadian taxpayers owe. We are just borrowing money to pay interest on the debt that was created, starting back in 1972, 1973, and 1974. That is my first question. Will they in future act in the same fiscally irresponsible fashion?
My second question is this. In 1979 the NDP moved a motion of non-confidence in the Conservative Government. The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was the Minister of Finance. Every reputable economic group in the country said that his 1979 Budget was the fairest Budget to the poor people of Canada in the entire decade. When the NDP had clout in a minority Government they did not produce Budgets that were fair to poor people. This Party produced one in 1979 and they threw us out of office. We have a right to know, as do Canadian taxpayers, whether they will act in that fashion in the future to punish the poor of the country? Will they act in a fashion designed to increase the debt load for future generations instead of being fiscally responsible?
